newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa grapples with insider trading.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa grapples with insider trading.

text.p: South Africa, burdened with a reputation as a haven of insider trading, could introduce legislation by year-end to tackle unfair dealing in stocks and bonds, industry leaders said on Monday.

Mervyn King, chairman of a government-appointed task group on insider trading set up by former Finance Minister Chris Liebenberg last year, said his committee would deliver its proposals to the finance ministry within six weeks.
Legislation based on its recommendations could be passed late this year or early in 1998, although this was a matter for government, he added.
Insider trading, never far from the surface in South African markets, is back in the spotlight following the apparent leaking of news of a big shake-up at car firm Automakers Ltd earlier this month.
Its share price shot up ahead of news that majority shareholder Sankorp would make a payout to minorities at a substantial premium to the prevailing market price.

"The committee's recommendations, if implemented, will hopefully try and solve some of these insider trading problems -- and not just for equities, but also for bonds and derivatives, too," King told Reuters.
"Things like the Automakers incident indicate that it is a serious problem, although it is very difficult to measure."
Insider trading is a criminal offence in South Africa, with penalties of up to 10 years in prison and fines of up to 500,000 rand ($110,000). But there has never been a conviction.

Richard Connellan, executive director of the Securities Regulation Panel (SRP), the watchdog charged with overseeing fair dealing, blames current inadequate legislation, particularly the onus to prove a case beyond all reasonable doubt under criminal law.

"The panel believes there should be changes to the law. Proving beyond reasonable doubt is exceptionally difficult in matters such as securities dealing where there is in fact a lot of subjectivity," he said.
Industry sources said the SRP was investigating the Automakers deal, although Connellan declined to comment.

The SRP is believed to have lodged at least three "very strong" cases of alleged insider trading, they said, but the Attorney-General was unlikely to seek to prosecute in any of them because of weaknesses in the law.

Johannesburg Stock Exchange executive president Roy Andersen agreed. "We think the legislation is inherently defective and that's why the Securities Regulation Panel has not succeeded in a prosecution," he said.
A further handicap of present insider trading regulations is that they deal only with price-sensitive information concerning companies.
The JSE hopes to address some of the problems with the launch of the Stock Exchange News Service (SENS) by the middle of this year.
Modelled on the London bourse's Regulatory News Service, SENS would require the real-time dissemination of all relevant and price-sensitive information relating to listed companies.
SENS may help, but its advent will still leave open the issue of price-sensitive information concerning bonds or derivatives, such as stock index contracts.
Many dealers believe key economic indicators are also routinely leaked to certain market players, something which can give an unfair advantage in the government bond market in particular.
Until the loopholes are tightened, individual investors will continue to suffer, according to David Sylvester, chairman of the Shareholders' Association of South Africa.

"Obviously it is a serious concern. It's a pity it takes a case like Automakers to bring insider trading into the spotlight -- it should be there all the time because it happens on a weekly basis," he said. ($=4.58 rand)
